stimulus.text: "I left these shores a red-hot imperialist. I wanted the American eagle to go screaming into the Pacific. … But I have thought some more, since then, and I have seen that we do not intend to free, but to subjugate the people of the Philippines. … It should, it seems to me, be our pleasure and duty to make these people free, and let them deal with their own domestic questions in their own way. And so I am an anti-imperialist. I am opposed to having the eagle put its talons on any other land." — Mark Twain, quoted in the New York World, October 15, 1900

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt from Mark Twain, quoted in the New York World, October 15, 1900, public domain.

rationales.A: Twain opposes the eagle seizing any other land. Hawaii was annexed in 1898, and his phrase covers it too.
rationales.B: The eagle here is American power seizing land, not trade. Twain's image is about conquest, not commerce.
rationales.C: Talons seize prey. Twain's image says empire is a bird of prey grabbing land, which is conquest dressed up as liberation.
rationales.D: Twain opposed seizing any other land. Joining the scramble for Africa is the opposite of his position.
rationales.general:
1. Read the image. Talons seize prey; an eagle's talons do not free anything.
2. Connect it to the passage. Twain has just said America means to subjugate, not free, the Philippines.
3. Test the other readings. Trade, Hawaii's annexation as a good, and an African scramble all miss the image's point.
4. Put it together. The metaphor is Twain's verdict: what expansionists called liberation was conquest.
Remember: a writer's metaphor is an argument in disguise, so translate the image back into a claim.
